summaries.example: Imagine a banana on a kitchen counter. On Monday it is green, and on Friday it is brown and soft. A temporal-parts philosopher might say the banana has an earlier part that is green and a later part that is brown. Another philosopher might say it is one whole banana that changes over time.
summaries.summary: The entry asks how things remain the same while time passes. One answer says that things have temporal parts, rather like having spatial parts. On this view, a person might have a yesterday-part, a today-part, and a tomorrow-part. Another answer says that a person is wholly present at each time, even though the person’s features and smaller parts can change. The first view is called perdurance, and the second is called endurance. The debate is used to study change, objects that share a location, unclear beginnings and endings, and the connection between time and space. Philosophers disagree about whether physics supports temporal parts, and about whether people have them. The entry presents arguments on both sides rather than choosing a final winner.
key_ideas: Some philosophers compare lasting through time with taking up space. A person can have a head and feet in different places, and might also have different time-parts at different times.
Perdurantists believe ordinary things have temporal parts. Endurantists believe ordinary things are whole at each time and do not have temporal parts.
Temporal parts may offer an explanation of change: different time-parts can have different properties.
Philosophers also use this debate to think about objects that seem to share a place, such as a statue and the clay forming it.
There is no settled answer. Each side has different ways to explain change, shared places, and fuzzy beginnings or endings.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us ask what it means for something to stay the same. It connects everyday puzzles—like an aging banana, a repaired bicycle, or a clay statue—to bigger questions about time, change, identity, and what kinds of things exist.

important_terms.definition: A part of a thing that exists during a particular time, such as a person’s yesterday-part or a banana’s Monday-part.
The view that an ordinary thing lasts by having different temporal parts at different times.
The view that an ordinary thing lasts as a whole and is completely present whenever it exists.
The way one thing can share a place with another thing, such as a clay lump and a statue made from it.

questions_to_think_about: Is the banana on Monday the very same whole banana as the one on Friday?
Would you rather describe yourself as having a yesterday-part and a today-part, or as one whole person who changes?
Can two different things be in exactly the same place?
If a bicycle is slowly rebuilt, when does it stop being the same bicycle?

summaries.example: Suppose a lump of clay is shaped into a statue on Wednesday and smashed on Sunday. The lump existed before the statue and may survive after it, so they appear to be different objects that occupy the same place while the statue exists. A perdurantist can say that the statue is a shorter four-dimensional object sharing some temporal parts with the longer-lived lump. An endurantist may instead say that the two objects wholly coincide, with the lump constituting the statue but not being identical to it.
summaries.summary:
Temporal-parts theories address persistence: how an object can exist at more than one time while remaining the same object. Perdurantists hold that ordinary objects are extended through time and possess temporal parts. Endurantists hold that ordinary objects endure by being wholly present whenever they exist. The dispute is ontological, but it also concerns location, explanation, and the meaning of claims about an object at a time. Perdurantists argue that temporal parts clarify temporary intrinsic properties: an earlier part can be unripe and a later part overripe. Endurantists respond with alternatives, including relations between objects and times, adverbial accounts of how properties are had, and presentism. Neither side has a universally accepted solution.

The debate also appears in coincidence puzzles. A statue and a lump of clay can seem both distinct and co-located. Perdurantism can model temporary coincidence through shared temporal parts, while an endurantist standard account says that constitution is not identity. Permanent coincidence is more difficult for temporal-parts theories because the objects share all their temporal parts; modal differences may then do the explanatory work. Questions about vagueness, time, relativity, universal composition, and personal identity add further complications. The entry presents these as interconnected but unsettled philosophical problems.
key_ideas: Perdurantism treats persistence as a kind of four-dimensional extension: an object has spatial parts and temporal parts. Endurantism treats persistence differently: the whole object is present at each time.
Temporal parts are proposed partly to explain temporary properties. An earlier part of a banana can be unripe while a later part is overripe, without one part having both properties.
Critics argue that this may describe variation rather than genuine change, since the whole four-dimensional object and its temporal parts may each be unchanging in an atemporal description.
Coincidence cases, such as a statue and its clay, motivate competing explanations. Perdurantists use overlapping temporal parts; endurantists may use constitution or other accounts.
Views about the nature of time do not map neatly onto views about persistence. Presentism, eternalism, and growing-universe theories create different pressures, but no simple pairing is forced.
Special relativity is sometimes taken to favor perdurance because simultaneity depends on a frame of reference. The entry stresses that this does not by itself provide a conclusive argument.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate tests competing ideas about identity, properties, time, and composition. It also shows how a single puzzle can support several theories, each with costs. The consequences reach beyond physical objects: they bear on personal survival, responsibility, the persistence of institutions and artworks, and ways of representing changing entities in applied ontology.

important_terms.definition: The theory that persisting objects have temporal parts and extend through time in a way analogous to how they extend through space.
The theory that a persisting object is wholly present at every time at which it exists and lacks temporal parts.
A part of an object located during a time or interval; some theories include instantaneous time-slices, while others include longer temporal segments.
The metaphysical question of what exists, including whether ordinary objects have temporal parts.
The puzzle of explaining how one object can have apparently incompatible properties at different times, such as being unripe and overripe.
A case in which distinct objects occupy the same place, either temporarily or throughout their existence.
The view that two coinciding objects can be distinct because one constitutes the other without being identical to it.
The view that any collection of objects has a composite object, or sum; it is often linked with four-dimensional theories and many possible temporal combinations.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining a banana’s different properties by assigning them to different temporal parts explain change, or merely redescribe it?
Should a statue and the lump of clay composing it count as one object or two? What would determine the answer?
Would a theory of persistence be easier if only present things existed?
If a person’s brain were divided between two bodies, what would each resulting person’s relation to the original be?
Can a scientific theory about spacetime settle a metaphysical dispute about parts and identity?

summaries.example: A bicycle you receive from a relative is repaired over several years. Many parts are replaced, and later some old parts are used in another bicycle. Which bicycle, if either, is the original? A perdurantist might describe several four-dimensional objects with different temporal parts. An endurantist might say one whole bicycle continues through the repairs, or might use a different account of what makes it the same bicycle.
summaries.summary:
Temporal parts are proposed as a way to understand persistence: the fact that a thing exists at different times. The idea resembles spatial parts. A person occupies different places through different spatial parts, such as a head and feet; perhaps the person also occupies different times through temporal parts, such as a person-yesterday and a person-today. Perdurantism accepts this picture. Endurantism says instead that ordinary objects are wholly present whenever they exist and do not have temporal parts.

The disagreement matters because objects change. A banana can be unripe at one time and overripe at another. Perdurantists assign these properties to different temporal parts. Endurantists may explain them by saying the banana has different relations to different times, has properties in different ways, or exists only in the present. The entry also examines coincidence. A lump of clay and a statue seem distinct in some respects but occupy the same place. Temporal-parts theories can explain this through shared temporal parts; an influential endurantist approach says the lump constitutes the statue without being identical to it. Further problems involve vague beginnings and endings, theories of time, relativity, and the persistence of people. The source presents several arguments and replies, with no final agreement.
key_ideas: The central question is how objects persist through time and what makes them the same object at different times.
Perdurantists compare time with space: just as a person has spatial parts, a person may have time-parts such as a yesterday-part and a today-part.
Endurantists reject that comparison and say the whole object exists at each time, even though its smaller parts and properties can change.
Temporal parts are offered as a solution to the problem of change, but critics say they may only describe different states instead of explaining genuine change.
Coincidence puzzles challenge the idea that two different objects cannot share one location. Both major theories have strategies for handling these cases.
Theories of time and theories of persistence may influence each other, but the entry does not treat any pairing as automatic or settled.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about temporal parts helps clarify what we mean by “the same thing” across change. It connects ordinary cases—repairs, aging, and making statues—with deep questions about whether objects are three-dimensional or four-dimensional, how time works, and whether scientific theories support particular metaphysical views.

important_terms.definition: The view that things continue to exist by having different temporal parts at different times.
The view that a thing continues as a whole, without temporal parts, and is wholly present at each time it exists.
A time-related portion of a persisting thing, such as a tree during one year or a person at one moment.
A puzzle in which two objects seem to occupy one place at the same time, as with a statue and its clay.
A relation in which one object, such as a lump of clay, makes up another object, such as a statue, without being the very same object.
The view that past, present, and future things all exist.
The view that only present things, events, and states exist.
Uncertainty or lack of a sharp boundary, such as not knowing exactly when a crumbling building stops existing.

questions_to_think_about: When a bicycle is repaired piece by piece, what facts should decide whether it remains the same bicycle?
Does saying that an earlier temporal part is green and a later one is yellow really explain how one object changes color?
Could a statue and its lump of clay be two objects in one place without creating extra weight?
Does the existence of the past and future make temporal parts more plausible?
What might happen to a theory of personal identity if one person could divide into two future people?
